name: Finance English
lede: Talk about numbers, forecasts, and risk without hiding behind jargon. Learn the finance words that keep a meeting honest — and make you sound like you actually own the numbers.
outcome: Speak plainly about forecasts, margins, and risk — and ask the questions that expose a weak number.
outcomes: Read a P&L or forecast and ask the two or three questions that actually matter.
Push back on a number that sounds too good — without sounding like you don’t trust the room.
Explain a variance, a shortfall, or a bad quarter in plain language the whole business understands.

aside.title: For the meeting where the numbers get questioned.
aside.body: Every term here is one you’ll hear in a forecast review, a budget call, or a board pack — explained the way a colleague would, not a textbook.

words.definition: The money a business brings in from selling its products or services.
words.example: Revenue grew nine per cent, but most of that came from one client.

words.definition: The money left from sales after paying the direct cost of delivering them.
words.example: Gross margin fell because our hosting costs doubled last quarter.

words.definition: What remains after all the costs of running the business are paid.
words.example: We made a profit, but far less than the plan promised.

words.definition: The movement of money in and out of a business over time.
words.example: Cash flow is tight, even though the order book looks strong.

words.definition: How quickly a company spends its cash before earning enough to cover costs.
words.example: At the current burn rate, we have eleven months of runway.

words.definition: The amount of money a team plans to spend over a period.
words.example: That project is over budget and only half finished.

words.definition: The gap between what you planned to spend or earn and what actually happened.
words.example: The biggest variance is in marketing spend, not headcount.

words.definition: The total ongoing cost of running a business, taken as one figure.
words.example: We need to take ten per cent out of our cost base.

words.definition: Regular costs of running a business that don’t depend on how much you sell.
words.example: Moving to a smaller office cut our overheads by a fifth.

words.definition: Money spent on long-term assets like equipment, buildings, or software.
words.example: The board approved the capex, but wants it phased over two years.

words.definition: The day-to-day running costs of a business, as opposed to long-term investment.
words.example: Opex is flat, which is a good result given the hiring.

words.definition: The gain you get from an investment, measured against what it cost.
words.example: The ROI on that campaign was weaker than we expected.

words.definition: The time it takes for an investment to earn back what it cost.
words.example: The payback is under two years, which makes it easy to approve.

words.definition: Removing an asset or debt from the books because it has lost its value.
words.example: We took a small write-off on the old equipment.

words.definition: A reduction in an asset’s recorded value because it is worth less now.
words.example: The auditor flagged an impairment on the software we bought.

words.definition: Money set aside in the accounts for a cost you expect to face.
words.example: We’ve made a provision for the legal costs.

words.definition: How easily a business can pay its bills with the cash it has.
words.example: Liquidity is fine for now, but not if the client pays late.

words.definition: A snapshot of what a company owns, owes, and is worth on a date.
words.example: The balance sheet looks healthy, but most of it is one building.

words.definition: A report showing sales, costs, and profit over a period of time.
words.example: Send me the P&L before the review on Thursday.

words.definition: Measured against the same period in the previous year.
words.example: Year-on-year growth is eight per cent, but the quarter was flat.

words.definition: To reach the point where income exactly covers all your costs.
words.example: We should break even by the third quarter next year.

words.definition: A company’s total sales, before any costs are taken out.
words.example: Top line growth is strong, but the profit is not there.

words.definition: The final profit figure, after every cost has been taken out.
words.example: The bottom line is that we missed the plan by six per cent.

words.definition: To predict future sales, costs, or cash from what you know now.
words.example: We forecast a slow first half, then a steady recovery.

words.definition: The pace a business is growing at, based on its recent results.
words.example: At this run rate, we’ll finish the year ahead of plan.

words.definition: A condition that makes growth harder, such as weak demand or higher costs.
words.example: Currency moves are a real headwind for the next two quarters.

words.definition: A condition that helps growth, such as rising demand or falling costs.
words.example: Cheaper shipping has been a tailwind for margins this year.

words.definition: The forecast a company gives the market about its expected results.
words.example: We held guidance, despite the weaker start to the quarter.
